C004.subject: raising the minimum wage
C004.object: employment in low-skill entry-level positions among teenagers in urban areas with high automation adoption
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: raising the minimum wage employment in low-skill entry-level positions among teenagers in urban areas with high automation adoption]

[PATH:empirical] Panel data from the Current Population Survey (CPS) merged with local minimum wage ordinances and Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) data on automation adoption (e.g., robot density per industry) for urban areas, 2010–2025 — Provides direct, high-frequency, geographically granular data to test the interaction effect of minimum wage increases and automation on teen employment in low-skill entry-level positions, allowing for difference-in-differences or event-study designs.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of minimum wage employment elasticities for teenagers, stratified by automation intensity (e.g., using industry-level robot adoption data from the International Federation of Robotics) — Synthesizes existing quasi-experimental studies to assess whether the negative employment effect is significantly larger in high-automation urban contexts, addressing heterogeneity and publication bias.

[PATH:empirical] Firm-level case studies or surveys of fast-food and retail chains in high-automation U.S. cities (e.g., San Francisco, Seattle) examining substitution of labor with kiosks or AI after minimum wage hikes — Provides mechanistic evidence of the substitution channel, testing whether minimum wage increases accelerate automation adoption specifically for entry-level tasks, thereby reducing teen employment.

scope.domain: low-skill labor markets with high minimum wage elasticity and high automation potential

qualifier.geographic: urban areas in the United States with high automation adoption

C005.subject: raising the minimum wage
C005.object: economic activity and demand, leading to stable or increased employment in low-skill entry-level positions
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: raising the minimum wage economic activity and demand, leading to stable or increased employment in low-skill entry-level positions]

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of minimum wage studies focusing on low-skill entry-level employment in urban developed economies during periods of moderate inflation and low unemployment (e.g., Card & Krueger revisited, or more recent work by Dube, Lester, Reich) — A systematic review of quasi-experimental studies in the specified scope can aggregate effect sizes and assess whether employment effects are stable or positive under the given temporal and geographic qualifiers.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal panel data from large urban labor markets (e.g., U.S. Current Population Survey or European Labour Force Survey) linked to state/city minimum wage changes, with controls for inflation and unemployment rates — Directly testing the hypothesis requires panel data that isolates the impact of minimum wage increases on employment and economic activity (e.g., consumer spending, small business revenue) while conditioning on moderate inflation and low unemployment conditions.

[PATH:theoretical] Simulation model of a low-skill labor market with high minimum wage elasticity, incorporating demand-side feedback from increased worker spending (e.g., a dynamic stochastic general equilibrium or agent-based model) — A formal model can clarify the conditions under which increased labor costs are offset by higher demand, helping to confirm or refute the proposed causal mechanism when empirical data are limited or noisy.

scope.domain: low-skill labor markets with high minimum wage elasticity

qualifier.temporal: during periods of moderate inflation and low unemployment
qualifier.geographic: in urban labor markets within developed economies

C006.subject: raising the minimum wage
C006.object: aggregate consumer demand and reduces turnover costs only when the wage increase is at least 20% above the current local median wage
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: raising the minimum wage aggregate consumer demand and reduces turnover costs only when the wage increase is at least 20% above the current local median wage]

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental studies comparing service industry outcomes in urban U.S. counties with high cost of living (index >110) that implemented minimum wage increases of ≥20% above local median wage vs. those with smaller or no increases, using synthetic control or difference-in-differences methods on BLS and county-level employment data post-2020. — Directly tests the threshold effect (≥20% above median) on consumer demand (e.g., retail sales, foot traffic) and turnover costs (e.g., quit rates, hiring costs) in the specified scope and qualifiers.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of minimum wage research focusing on labor demand elasticity and turnover, with subgroup analysis by wage increase magnitude relative to local median wage and local labor market tightness (e.g., unemployment rate <4%), drawn from peer-reviewed economics journals (e.g., Journal of Labor Economics, ILR Review). — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether a 20% threshold is consistently associated with positive demand and turnover effects, controlling for publication bias and heterogeneous contexts.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical model of monopsonistic competition in tight labor markets, incorporating consumer spending multipliers and firm-level turnover cost functions, calibrated to post-2020 U.S. urban service sector data. — Provides a causal mechanism explaining why a large relative wage increase (>20% above median) might uniquely stimulate aggregate demand (via higher worker spending) and reduce turnover (via efficiency wage effects) in settings with labor shortages, while smaller increases may not overcome offsetting price or substitution effects.

scope.domain: service industries with tight local labor markets

qualifier.temporal: post-2020 economic conditions with labor shortages
qualifier.geographic: urban counties in the United States with a cost of living index above 110

C007.subject: raising the minimum wage
C007.object: employment and increases operational costs for businesses
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: raising the minimum wage employment and increases operational costs for businesses]

[PATH:empirical] Cengiz, D., Dube, A., Lindner, A., & Zipperer, B. (2019). The effect of minimum wages on low-wage jobs. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 134(3), 1405-1454. — This study uses a quasi-experimental design across U.S. states to estimate employment effects of minimum wage increases, directly relevant to the service industry and local labor market conditions.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of minimum wage impacts on firm operating costs and employment in service industries, focusing on tight labor markets (e.g., meta-analysis by Wolfson & Belman, 2019, or similar). — A meta-analysis synthesizing multiple studies can clarify whether the predicted negative employment effect holds specifically in tight local labor markets and service sectors, addressing the scope of the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Card, D., & Krueger, A. B. (1994). Minimum wages and employment: A case study of the fast-food industry in New Jersey and Pennsylvania. American Economic Review, 84(4), 772-793. — This classic natural experiment examines minimum wage effects in a service industry (fast food) with tight local labor markets, providing direct evidence on employment and operational cost dynamics.

scope.domain: service industries with tight local labor markets
